summary: Highlights outstanding architectural issues about deploying and using QoS mechanisms in the Internet, and where further standards work may help. It is the outcome of a collaborative exercise.

plainLanguage.summary: Quality of service means giving some traffic a better deal than the plain, unpredictable service the Internet normally offers. Two designs exist for doing this, and this memo compares them and lists the twelve areas where work is still needed. It is a review by the Internet Architecture Board, not a specification.

questions: what is qos in the internet
how do integrated services and differentiated services differ
why is qos hard to deploy
how does tcp interact with qos
subtitle: A review of the two Internet quality-of-service architectures and the twelve areas where work is still needed.

tldr.problem: Quality of service means giving some traffic a better deal than the plain best-effort service the Internet offers. Two architectures exist, and both leave problems that block wide deployment.
tldr.mechanism: The memo compares the reservation-based Integrated Services model with the marking-based Differentiated Services model, then lists the twelve areas that need work: applications, the service environment, discovery, routing and resource management, TCP, packet classifiers, the service set, measurement, accounting, deployment diversity, inter-domain signalling and deployment logistics.
tldr.outcome: Its conclusion is that no single architecture will do. A tailored mix, aggregates in the core and per-flow treatment at the edge, is the direction it points to. The memo is Informational and is the outcome of an Internet Architecture Board exercise.

today: RFC 2990 is an Informational memo, the outcome of an Internet Architecture Board exercise, and the metadata does not list it as obsoleted or updated. It describes the state of QoS architecture work in November 2000 and names the areas that still needed standards work. It is read with RFC 1633 for the Integrated Services overview and RFC 2475 for the Differentiated Services architecture.

sections.title: Best Effort and What QoS Adds
sections.content:
The default service offering associated with the Internet is a best-effort variable service response. Within that profile the network makes no attempt to actively differentiate its service response between the traffic streams generated by concurrent users, and the response varies as the load generated by the active traffic flows varies.

The objective of Internet Quality of Service efforts is to augment this base service with a number of selectable service responses. These may be distinguished from the best-effort service by some form of superior service level, or by providing a predictable service response that is unaffected by external conditions such as the number of concurrent traffic flows.

Any network service response is an outcome of the resources available to service a load, and of the level of the load itself. To offer a distinguished service there is therefore not only a requirement to provide a differentiated service response within the network, but also a requirement to control the service-qualified load admitted into the network, so that the resources allocated to support a particular response are capable of providing it for the imposed load. The memo calls this combination rules plus behaviours. In the terminology of the Differentiated Services architecture, the admission control function is undertaken by a traffic conditioner, an entity that performs traffic conditioning functions and may contain meters, markers, droppers and shapers, and whose actions are governed by explicit or implicit admission control agents.

The memo names the service load control aspect of QoS as perhaps the most troubling component of the architecture. There is a wide array of well understood service response mechanisms available to IP networks, but matching a set of such mechanisms within a controlled environment to respond to a set of service loads so as to achieve a completely consistent service response remains an area of weakness within existing IP QoS architectures.
sections.plainLanguage: The normal Internet gives every packet the same, unpredictable treatment. QoS tries to give some traffic a guaranteed or better service. That needs two things: a way to treat that traffic differently, and a way to stop too much of it entering the network.

sections.title: Two Ways to Control the Load
sections.content:
One way to control the imposed load is an application-driven process of service level negotiation, also known as application-signalled QoS. The application first signals its service requirements to the network and the network responds. The application proceeds if the network has indicated that it can carry the additional load at the requested service level. If the network indicates that it cannot accommodate the requirements, the application may proceed in any case, on the basis that the network will service the data on a best effort basis.

This approach can be used within the Integrated Services architecture, where the application frames its service request within the resource reservation protocol RSVP. The network can either commit to the service profile with a resource reservation or reject the request. There is no requirement for the application to reconfirm the reservation periodically, because the interaction between RSVP and the network constantly refreshes the reservation while it remains active. The reservation stays in force until the application explicitly asks for it to be terminated, or the network signals that it cannot continue.

The alternative is to decouple the network load control function from the application, which is the basis of the Differentiated Services architecture. The network admits no more traffic within each service category than there are assumed resources to deliver the intended response. There is necessarily some imprecision, because traffic may take an arbitrary path through the network. The application requests a service by marking each packet with a code indicating the desired service, with no prior negotiation. This decouples the end systems from the network and lets the operator moderate the workload placed on the network's resources without reference to individual requests from end systems.

These two approaches are the endpoints of a continuum. The fine-grained per application invocation reservation model can be aggregated into larger, more general and potentially more approximate aggregate reservation states, and the end-to-end element-by-element reservation control can be progressively approximated by treating a collection of subnetworks or an entire transit network as an aggregate service element.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two designs. In one, the application asks the network for a service and the network says yes or no. In the other, the application simply labels its packets and the network deals with them as best it can. The first is precise and expensive; the second scales and is approximate.

sections.title: The Outstanding Architectural Issues
sections.content:
Both architectures have elements that appear to be acting as deterrents to widespread deployment. The memo lists the outstanding work.

Applications: whether QoS is a per-application service, a transport-layer option, or both, is uncertain. A transport-layer option needs no change to the application, but the application cannot tell the network what it needs, so the network may provide a response far superior to the application's true requirements or far inferior to what it needs. In the Integrated Services model the application must supply a profile of its anticipated traffic and accept being policed to fit inside it. In the Differentiated Services model there is no explicit provision for the application to talk to the network about service levels at all, so if a boundary traffic conditioner enters a load shedding state the application is not signalled. Receiver capability negotiation is also needed, because there is no value in the sender establishing a quality-enabled path to a receiver that cannot absorb the flow.

The service environment: there appears to be no single comprehensive service environment that possesses both service accuracy and scaling properties. Integrated Services state and RSVP signalling are not cost effective, or even feasible, to operate per application across the high speed core of a network. Differentiated Services scales well, but the lack of end-to-end signalling makes it an approach that cannot operate in isolation. The memo says what is required is resource availability signalling from the core of the network to the boundary, and some form of signalling from the boundary to the client application.

Discovery and routing: there is no robust mechanism for network path discovery with specific service performance attributes, and both architectures assume the best effort routing path is used. QoS routing has been developed at some distance from the QoS architecture, and there is no explicit architectural option to align the service path along anything other than the single best routing metric path. The memo argues that single path selection with static load characteristics does not match a networked environment with a richer mesh of connectivity and dynamic load, and that per-path dynamic load metrics are needed so that incoming traffic can be distributed across a broader collection of network links.

TCP: a rate-adaptive flow such as TCP uses the feedback from the ACK packet stream to time subsequent data transmissions, so the flow rate is an outcome of the service quality given to both the forward data packets and the reverse ACK packets. If the ACK stream is treated with a different service profile from the data packets, it remains an open question to what extent throughput is compromised. High jitter on the ACK stream causes ACK compression, which causes high burst rates on the subsequent send, which stresses the service capacity of the network and compromises TCP throughput. Token bucket traffic conditioners, which are typical of QoS architectures, impose tail drop behaviour on TCP streams, and that can produce TCP timeout retransmission and unduly penalise the average TCP goodput rate.

Classifiers: both architectures use packet classifiers. Fine-grained classifiers isolate the elements of traffic from one invocation of an application, typically using the source and destination IP addresses and the source and destination port addresses. Coarse-grained classifiers isolate traffic that belongs to an aggregated service state, typically using the Differentiated Services code field. IP security, address translation and tunnels occlude the flow identification, and IP fragmentation means trailing fragments carry no TCP or UDP port information, so they can be classified into the base best effort category and delay delivery of the packet. The memo's advice is that applications should perform path MTU discovery to avoid fragmentation, and that encryption, header translation and header encapsulation should be deployed with due attention to their impact on service delivery classifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo lists what is missing. Applications cannot tell the network what they need, and are not told when the network cannot deliver. There is no way to find a path that can carry a particular service. Traffic conditioners that drop packets, as QoS ones do, hurt TCP badly. And encryption, address translation and fragmentation all hide the flow identity the network needs to classify traffic.

sections.title: Service Sets, Measurement, Accounting and Deployment
sections.content:
The service set: how many distinguished service responses are adequate? Differentiated Services puts no limiting restriction on the number of services an operator can offer. The operator is limited to a choice of up to 64 discrete services in terms of the 6 bit service code point in the IP header, but because the mapping from service to code point can be defined by each operator, there can be any number of potential services. A large number leads to end-to-end service coherency problems across multiple network domains, so the memo points to defining a small core set of service profiles as well-known and placing all other profiles within a private use category.

Measuring service delivery: a QoS architecture needs network management that gives a coherent view of the operating state of the network, in particular the resources available along a particular path, mapped to an admission control function that can decide whether to admit a flow along that path. The operator also needs to measure the operating parameters of the delivered service, both to substantiate the claim that the delivered quality conformed to the specifications and to let the client measure the delivered quality so that any premium can be justified.

Accounting: premium service is likely to attract a tariff increment, so some accounting of the use of premium service tied to a particular client would appear to be necessary. No definition of such an accounting model, nor of how to gather the data, exists. The memo notes that the introduction of QoS services is a strong impetus to move from tariffs based on the characteristics of access to usage-based tariffs, which in turn requires metering resource use.

Deployment diversity and inter-domain signalling: it is extremely improbable that any single form of service differentiation technology will be rolled out across the Internet and across all enterprise networks. Some networks will deploy some form of it and others will not, some platforms will interoperate seamlessly and others less so. In such a heterogeneous environment, service capability discovery becomes as critical as being able to invoke service responses and measure the outcomes. Inter-domain routing adds a further dimension to the policy space, because a provider may have one interconnection agreement for best effort traffic and another for service qualified traffic, so external route advertisements would need to be qualified by accepted service profiles, and the number of objects managed by routing systems expands dramatically.

Deployment logistics: which gets built first, host applications or network infrastructure? No network operator will make the significant investment unless there are clients and applications ready to make immediate use of the facilities. Clients will not invest in enhanced services unless they see performance gains. No application designer will integrate service quality features unless there is a model of operation supported by widespread deployment that makes the extra complexity worthwhile. With every part of the deployment scenario waiting for the others to move, widespread deployment may require some other external impetus.
sections.plainLanguage: The remaining questions are practical ones. How many service levels should a network offer, how can the operator prove the service was delivered, how should premium service be billed, and how does quality travel between operators who each have their own agreements? On top of that, nobody will build the network unless someone is ready to use it, and nobody will build the application unless the network exists.

sections.title: The Objective and an End-to-End Model
sections.content:
The memo asks what precise problem QoS is attempting to solve, and answers by listing the intentions: to control the network service response so that the response to a specific service element is consistent and predictable; to control it so that a service element is provided with a level of response equal to or above a guaranteed minimum; to allow a service element to establish in advance the service response that can or will be obtained from the network; to control the contention for network resources such that a service element is provided with a superior level of network resource; to control contention such that a service element does not obtain an unfair allocation of resources; and to allow for efficient total utilization of network resources while servicing a spectrum of directed network service outcomes.

The first three are application-centric and the latter two network-centric, and the memo says none of them can be addressed in isolation. Within the end-to-end architectural model of the Internet, applications make minimal demands on the underlying IP network: in the case of TCP, the protocol uses an end-to-end control signal to adjust dynamically to the prevailing network state. QoS architectures add a different constraint, in that the network is placed in an active role within the task of resource allocation and service delivery, rather than being a passive object that requires end systems to adapt.

The memo then sketches how an end-to-end model might be built by combining both architectures, with IntServ letting applications interact with the network and DiffServ managing admission of the network's resources. The basic tension is between the per-application view of IntServ and the boundary-centric view of DiffServ. One building block is a service signalling protocol, and RSVP is the candidate: in its abstracted model it is a discovery signalling protocol that lets an application use a single transaction to communicate its service requirements to both the network and the remote party, and lets those network elements commit to the requirements. The barrier is that an element-by-element approach to service commitment implies per-flow signalling and per-flow processing for high precision services, which imposes an unacceptable level of overhead on the central core elements of large carrier networks. The DiffServ approach instead creates an external view of a compound network as a single subnetwork, with ingress and egress as two boundary service points, which removes the requirement for per-flow state and processing in the interior and provides aggregate service responses instead.

The conclusions say none of this is a reason to condemn the QoS architectures, nor a reason to believe the efforts will not come to fruition. The direction that appears most promising is not universal adoption of a single architecture, but a tailored approach, with aggregated service elements in the core of a network where scalability is a major design objective and per-flow service elements at the edge where accuracy of the service response is a sustainable outcome. Architecturally, that points to no single QoS architecture, but to a set of QoS mechanisms and a number of ways these mechanisms can be configured to interoperate in a stable and consistent fashion.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo lists what quality of service is meant to achieve: a predictable response, a guaranteed minimum, the ability to ask in advance, a fair share of resources, and efficient use of them. It then suggests a mix of the two designs, with per-flow treatment at the edge of the network and aggregated treatment in the core.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Internet is not an architecture that includes a strict implementation of fairness of access to the common transmission and switching resource. The introduction of any form of fairness, and in the case of QoS weighted fairness, implies a requirement for transparency in the implementation of the fairness contract between the network provider and the network's users. That requires some form of resource accounting and auditing, which in turn requires the use of authentication and access control. The balancing factor is that a shared resource should not overtly expose the level of resource usage of any one user to any other, so some level of secrecy is required in this environment.

The QoS environment also exposes the potential of theft of resources through the unauthorized admission of traffic with an associated service profile. Signalling protocols intended to undertake resource management and admission control therefore require the use of identity authentication and integrity protection.

Both forms of QoS architecture require the internal elements of the network to classify traffic based on identification carried in the packet header in the clear. Classification systems that use multi-field specifiers, or per-flow specifiers, rely on end-to-end packet header fields being carried in the clear, which conflicts with security architectures that attempt to mask such identifiers within an encrypted payload.

Finally, in the event of a rapid change in resource availability, such as a disaster, it is an undesirable outcome if the remaining resources are completely allocated to a single class of service to the exclusion of all other classes. The memo notes that such an outcome constitutes a denial of service, where the traffic control system selects paths that are incapable of carrying any traffic of a particular service class.
sections.plainLanguage: Fairness has to be visible to the operator, which means accounting and auditing, which means authentication and access control. Signalling that admits traffic has to be authenticated so nobody can take resources they have not paid for. And the classification the network does needs to see the packet header, which encryption hides.

   guaranteed minimum.

-  To allow a service element to establish in advance the service
   response that can or will be obtained from the network.

-  To control the contention for network resources such that a
   service element is provided with a superior level of network
   resource.

-  To control the contention for network resources such that a
   service element does not obtain an unfair allocation of
   resources (to some definition of 'fairness').

-  To allow for efficient total utilization of network resources
   while servicing a spectrum of directed network service outcomes.
